query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Zr and Hf content in the boride-based component will improve its resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion during hot-dip aluminum-plating by promoting a more stable microstructure and protective oxide formation.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard boride-based component without enhanced levels of Zr and Hf.
generation.intervention: Alloy the boride-based material with increased proportions of zirconium (Zr) and hafnium (Hf).
generation.conditions: The component is exposed to molten aluminum under operating temperatures typical of hot-dip plating; the temperature and time exposure remain within ranges where the high-entropy boride maintains a single-phase hexagonal structure.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a chemically homogeneous, single-phase hexagonal structure with improved microstructural stability that promotes the development of stable, protective oxide layers.
generation.mechanism: The increased Zr and Hf content enhances thermal-oxidative resistance by facilitating the formation of stable compounds and protective oxide layers, which in turn reduce the penetration and aggressive attack of molten aluminum on the component. Additionally, improved microstructure minimizes porosity that could serve as corrosion initiation sites.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline material, the Zr/Hf-enriched component will exhibit reduced mass loss and less surface degradation when exposed to molten aluminum, indicating improved corrosion resistance.
generation.baseline: Conventional boride-based components with standard Zr and Hf concentrations, which show lower thermal-oxidative resistance and are more susceptible to molten-aluminum corrosion.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected provided that the increase in Zr and Hf content does not compromise other mechanical properties, and the operating conditions (temperature and exposure time) do not exceed the range where the high-entropy boride phase remains stable.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether the enhanced thermal-oxidative resistance observed in gas-dynamic tests directly translates to improved molten-aluminum corrosion performance, given potential differences in corrosion mechanisms between oxidative and molten-metal environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of boride-based samples: one with conventional composition and one modified by increasing Zr and Hf content. Subject both groups to identical molten-aluminum exposure conditions mimicking hot-dip plating operations, controlling for temperature, time, and atmosphere.
measurements: Mass loss measurements before and after exposure
Surface morphology analysis via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
Phase composition analysis using X-ray diffraction (XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr/Hf-enriched samples do not show statistically significant reductions in mass loss and surface degradation, or if no improvement in phase stability is detected compared to the conventional samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
This manuscript shows the study of the structure, mechanical, and chemical properties of high-entropy borides MeB2 (Me = Ti, Ta, Nb, Hf, Zr). High-entropy borides were synthesized by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering. A chemically homogeneous powder with a low iron content (0.12%) was obtained in a planetary mill by rotating the planetary disk/pots at 200–400 rpm and a processing time of 7.5 h. The structure, mechanical, and chemical properties of the resulting high-entropy borides have been studied. A single-phase hexagonal structure is formed during spark plasma sintering of mechanically alloyed powders at 2000 °C. The microhardness of the samples ranged from 1763 to 1959 HV. Gas-dynamic tests of the synthesized materials showed that an increase in the content of Zr and Hf in the composition increases the thermal-oxidative resistance of the material.
